en: Itivuttaka 49 Dukanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said. This is the second discourse in the section on pairs. It has been said by the Blessed One, said by the Well-Gone One, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The person who is a speaker of what is beneficial and the person who is a doer of what is beneficial. These, monks, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, it was said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world…’ Now, Bhante, how is it that a person is a speaker of what is beneficial? "It is when a person, having learned the Dhamma—whether discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous accounts, or questions-and-answers—teaches it to others extensively and in detail, elucidates it, analyzes it, and clarifies it; and when he is asked a question about the meaning, he answers it properly and thoroughly. In this way, a person is a speaker of what is beneficial. "And how, Bhante, is a person a doer of what is beneficial? "It is when a person, having learned the Dhamma—whether discourses... or questions-and-answers—practices it accordingly, trains in accordance with it, and lives in conformity with it. In this way, a person is a doer of what is beneficial. "Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante! As if he were turning upright what had been overturned, or revealing what was hidden, or showing the way to one who was lost, or bringing an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—it has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. We go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. And those bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the words of the Blessed One. Thus was the second discourse in the section on pairs recited.
The Discourse on Views.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Bhikkhus, obsessed by two types of views, some gods and humans lag behind, while others run too far ahead; but those with vision see clearly."
And how, monks, do some lag behind?

Monks, gods and humans delight in existence, rejoice in existence, and find pleasure in existence; thus, when the Dhamma is being taught for the cessation of existence, their minds do not leap forward, do not become confident, do not settle, and do not resolve.
It is in this way, monks, that some lag behind.
And how, monks, do some overreach?
Some, being terrified, ashamed, and disgusted by existence itself, delight in non-existence:
"For indeed, sirs, when this self, with the breakup of the body after death, is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death."
"This is peaceful, this is sublime, this is the very truth.
In this way, monks, some run too far.
And how, monks, do those with vision see?
"Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees what has come to be as it really is.
Having seen what has come to be as it really is, he practices for disenchantment with what has come to be, for the fading away of lust for it, and for its cessation.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that those who possess vision see."
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Those who, having seen what has come to be as it truly is, ...”
And by transcending what has come to be,
they are liberated regarding things as they truly are,
through the complete exhaustion of craving for existence.
He indeed is one who has fully understood what has come to be,
free from craving for existence and non-existence;
through the dissolution of what has come to be, that bhikkhu—
"One does not come to renewed existence.
This meaning was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The twelfth [sutta].
The Second Chapter.
Its summary:
Two faculties, two things to be heated.
Two others by virtue;
lack of moral dread and hypocrisy—these two—along with the object of spiritual urgency: these make ten.
Thoughts, teaching, knowledge, wisdom,
and fifthly, the Dhamma;
the unborn, the arrow of the elements.
Training, and by means of wakefulness;
and by the view of non-self—
thus twenty-two [factors] have been proclaimed.
The Second Book is finished.
